name: Mixopterus (Sea Scorpion)
fact: A terrifying eurypterid with spiny front legs designed to snag soft-bodied prey. Larger than any modern scorpion, Mixopterus was one of the top predators of Ordovician seas. Its compound eyes gave it excellent underwater vision.

name: Cooksonia
fact: One of the very FIRST land plants ever! Just a tiny forking stem with spore capsules. It started transforming bare rock into soil. Everything green you see today ultimately descended from tiny plants like this.

name: Eurypterid (Peak Era)
fact: Sea scorpions hit their peak in the Silurian! Some could haul themselves onto land for short trips — the first animals to briefly visit land. They were absolutely terrifying and dominated for millions of years.

name: Early Jawed Fish (Acanthodian)
fact: The first fish with real jaws! This was a revolution. Suddenly fish could bite and hunt in totally new ways. All land animals with jaws — amphibians, reptiles, dinosaurs, mammals, and us — ultimately descended from early jawed fish like these.

name: Sea Lily (Crinoid)
fact: Beautiful flower-like creatures that were actually animals! They're related to starfish and sea urchins. They're still alive today in deep ocean, barely changed in 400 million years — living fossils.

name: Thelodus
fact: One of the first armored fish with a thick spiky skin. No jaws yet, but the beginnings of a real spine. Part of the long chain of fish evolution leading to us.

name: Brontoscorpio
fact: A giant sea scorpion whose single fossilized finger gave scientists enough evidence to calculate its monstrous size. Brontoscorpio could likely breathe both in water and during brief excursions on land - making it a terrifying prospect for the first small land-walking invertebrates.

name: Climatius
fact: A small but aggressive acanthodian fish bristling with spines along its belly and fins - earning acanthodians the nickname spiny sharks. Climatius had up to five pairs of paired fins, far more than any modern fish, and may represent an early experiment in limb evolution.

name: Cephalaspis
fact: A pancake-flat jawless fish with a broad head shield that scooped organic material off the seafloor. Sensory organs on its head shield could detect predator movement through subtle pressure changes in the water - an ancient version of the lateral line fish still use today.

name: Pterygotus (Giant Eurypterid)
fact: The largest arthropod ever discovered - a sea scorpion longer than a grown man. Armed with massive clawed chelicerae, Pterygotus was the apex predator of Silurian seas. Its paddle-like tail fin made it a fast agile swimmer that hunted primitive fish and nautiloids.

name: Eurypterus
fact: New York's state fossil and the best-known sea scorpion — thousands have been collected from the Bertie Waterlime, a lagoon that kept drying out.

name: Guiyu
fact: The oldest near-complete bony fish. It sits near the root of the lobe-finned fishes — the branch that includes lungfish, coelacanths and, eventually, us.

name: Entelognathus
fact: An armoured fish whose jaw bones match the ones in your own face. It showed that the bony jaw of humans traces back to placoderms.

name: Pneumodesmus
fact: A millipede with breathing holes along its body — so it breathed air. It is the oldest known animal confirmed to have lived on land.
know: Found by a bus driver and amateur collector, Mike Newman, in 2004. The spiracles — breathing pores — are what prove it lived out of the water.
debate: How old? First dated to about 428 million years; a 2017 study argued for about 414 million — which would make it Devonian, not Silurian.

name: Baragwanathia
fact: A club moss with leaves, surprisingly complex for so early. Its age was argued about for decades because it seemed far too advanced for the Silurian.

name: Aquilonifer
fact: A tiny arthropod that towed its babies behind it in capsules on long threads, like a child flying ten kites.
know: The Herefordshire fossils are preserved inside rock nodules in three dimensions. Scientists grind each nodule away a fraction of a millimetre at a time, photograph every layer, and rebuild the animal on a computer.

name: Haliestes
fact: A sea spider — not a true spider — preserved in full three dimensions, legs and all. Its family still lives on the seabed today.

name: Birkenia
fact: A small jawless fish covered in rows of thin, spiky scales. Its tail bent downward, the opposite of a shark's.

name: Slimonia
fact: A large sea scorpion whose tail ended in a serrated, spike-like blade.

name: Andreolepis
size: Small — known from scales and teeth
fact: One of the earliest ray-finned fishes — the group that today includes almost all fish you know, from goldfish to tuna.

name: Qilinyu
fact: An armoured fish with bony plates along its jaw edges in the same places as the jaw bones of your own face — a clue to where our jaws came from.

name: Megamastax
fact: “Big mouth”: the largest backboned animal known from its time, with sharp teeth for grabbing and blunt ones for crushing armoured prey.
know: A fish this big needs a lot of oxygen, so its discovery in 2014 was taken as a sign that the air already held plenty of it.
